w: בִּזְמַן שֶׁאִישׁ הַפַּח|while the Tin Woodman
s.line: While the Woodman was making a ladder from wood which he found in the forest Dorothy lay down and slept, for she was tired by the long walk.
s.note: נִשְׁכַּב (nif'al) = to lie down, the act of getting into position; שָׁכַב (pa'al) = to be lying, as Toto does in the next sentence. עָיֵף מִ… = tired from …: אֲנִי עָיֵף מֵהָעֲבוֹדָה.

s.line: The Lion also curled himself up to sleep and Toto lay beside him.
s.note: הִתְכַּרְבֵּל = to curl up, snuggle up, a hitpa'el with four root letters. It is the cozy word for wrapping up on the sofa: הִתְכַּרְבַּלְתִּי בִּשְׂמִיכָה (I snuggled up in a blanket). לְיָד = next to; לְיָדוֹ = next to him.

s.line: The Scarecrow watched the Woodman while he worked, and said to him:
s.note: הִסְתַּכֵּל בְּ… = to watch, look at something for a while; הִסְתַּכֵּל עַל is also common. Compare הִבִּיט בְּ…, a bit more literary.

s.line: “I cannot think why this wall is here, nor what it is made of.”
s.note: חוֹמָה is a big defensive or boundary wall, like a city wall (חוֹמוֹת יְרוּשָׁלַיִם); the wall of a room is קִיר. נִמְצָא (nif'al of מָצָא, find) is the everyday "is located": אֵיפֹה נִמְצֵאת הַתַּחֲנָה? (where is the station?). עָשׂוּי מִ… = made of.

s.line: “Rest your brains and do not worry about the wall,” replied the Woodman.
s.note: תֵּן לְ… לָנוּחַ = "let … rest": תֵּן (give) + infinitive is the usual "let": תֵּן לִי לַחְשֹׁב (let me think). אַל תִּדְאַג = don't worry: אַל + future is the negative command.

s.line: “When we have climbed over it, we shall know what is on the other side.”
s.note: After <t>כְּשֶׁ</t> about the future, Hebrew uses the future tense: <t>כְּשֶׁנְּטַפֵּס</t> "when we (will) climb", where English says "when we have climbed". <t>הַצַּד הַשֵּׁנִי</t> (the second side) is the normal way to say "the other side".

s.line: After a time the ladder was finished.
s.note: הֻשְׁלַם is hof'al, the passive of hif'il הִשְׁלִים (to complete): הוּא הִשְׁלִים אֶת הַסֻּלָּם → הַסֻּלָּם הֻשְׁלַם. You will see it in the news: הַבְּנִיָּה הֻשְׁלְמָה (construction was completed).

w: יַעֲשֶׂה אֶת הָעֲבוֹדָה|would do the job|~idiom
s.line: It looked clumsy, but the Tin Woodman was sure it was strong and would answer their purpose.
s.note: מְסֻרְבָּל = clumsy, cumbersome. It is used for things and also for wording: מִשְׁפָּט מְסֻרְבָּל (a clumsy sentence). יַעֲשֶׂה אֶת הָעֲבוֹדָה = "will do the job", as in English.

s.line: The Scarecrow waked Dorothy and the Lion and Toto, and told them that the ladder was ready.
s.note: הֵעִיר (hif'il) = to wake someone up; you may also know it as "to remark", and both are in daily use (הוּא הֵעִיר הֶעָרָה = he made a remark). To wake up yourself is הִתְעוֹרֵר. מוּכָן = ready: a hof'al participle, literally "prepared".

s.line: The Scarecrow climbed up the ladder first,
but he was so awkward that Dorothy had to follow close behind and keep him from falling off.
s.note: כְּדֵי שֶׁ… + future = "so that …": כְּדֵי שֶׁלֹּא יִפֹּל = so that he won't fall. מְגֻשָּׁם = awkward, clumsy in movement; it also means "materialistic", from גַּשְׁמִי (material, physical).

s.line: When he got his head over the top of the wall the Scarecrow said, “Oh, my!”
s.note: רֹאשׁ is both "head" and "top": רֹאשׁ הַחוֹמָה (the top of the wall), רֹאשׁ הָהָר (the mountaintop). It is also the head of an organization: רֹאשׁ הַמֶּמְשָׁלָה (the prime minister). וַאו is borrowed from English and is what Israelis really say for "Oh, my!".

s.line: “Go on,” exclaimed Dorothy.
s.note: תַּמְשִׁיךְ is the future "you will continue", used as a polite command. In speech the future is much more common than the true imperative הַמְשֵׁךְ.

s.line: So the Scarecrow climbed farther up and sat down on the top of the wall,
s.note: הִתְיַשֵּׁב (hitpa'el) = to sit down, the movement; יָשַׁב (pa'al) = to sit, be sitting. The same pair as נִשְׁכַּב / שָׁכַב in sentence 1.

s.line: and Dorothy put her head over and cried, “Oh, my!” just as the Scarecrow had done.
s.note: מֵעֵבֶר לְ… = on the other side of, beyond: מֵעֵבֶר לַיָּם (overseas). הוֹצִיא (hif'il of יָצָא, go out) = to take or put something out.

s.line: Then Toto came up, and immediately began to bark, but Dorothy made him be still.
s.note: הִשְׁתִּיק is the hif'il (causative) of שָׁתַק (to be silent): "made him be silent". The hif'il often means "make someone do X": צָחַק laugh → הִצְחִיק make laugh.

s.line: The Lion climbed the ladder next, and the Tin Woodman came last;

w: בָּרֶגַע שֶׁהֵצִיצוּ|the moment that they peeked|hif'il · צ־ו־ץ
s.line: but both of them cried, “Oh, my!” as soon as they looked over the wall.
s.note: בָּרֶגַע שֶׁ… = "the moment that, as soon as": תִּתְקַשֵּׁר בָּרֶגַע שֶׁתַּגִּיעַ (call as soon as you arrive). הֵצִיץ = to peek, take a quick look.

s.line: When they were all sitting in a row on the top of the wall, they looked down and saw a strange sight.
s.note: מַרְאֶה (a sight, an appearance) comes from the same root as רָאָה (saw), so רָאוּ מַרְאֶה is a verb and noun from one root, as in קָד קִידָה. A mirror is מַרְאָה, almost the same word.

s.line: Before them was a great stretch of country having a floor as smooth and shining and white as the bottom of a big platter.
s.note: הִשְׂתָּרֵעַ = to stretch out, extend (of land): in the hitpa'el, the ת of the prefix swaps places with a first root letter שׂ/ס/שׁ, as in הִסְתַּכֵּל. מַבְרִיק = shiny, from בָּרָק (lightning); in speech it also means "brilliant": רַעְיוֹן מַבְרִיק.

s.line: Scattered around were many houses made entirely of china and painted in the brightest colors.
s.note: Three pa'ul participles in a row: פָּזוּר (scattered), עָשׂוּי (made), צָבוּעַ (painted). חַרְסִינָה = china, porcelain; חֶרֶס is ordinary earthenware. A "bright" color is עַז (strong); בָּהִיר means light, pale.

s.line: These houses were quite small,
the biggest of them reaching only as high as Dorothy’s waist.
s.note: הַגָּדוֹל שֶׁבָּהֶם = "the biggest of them": the definite adjective plus שֶׁבָּהֶם makes a superlative without בְּיוֹתֵר. לְמַדַּי = fairly, rather. מָתְנַיִם (waist, hips) is a dual form, like רַגְלַיִם.

s.line: There were also pretty little barns, with china fences around them;
and many cows and sheep and horses and pigs and chickens, all made of china, were standing about in groups.
s.note: פֹּה וָשָׁם = here and there, a set phrase; note the vav pointed וָ. גְּדֵרוֹת חַרְסִינָה and פָּרַת חַרְסִינָה are construct chains used like adjectives ("china fences, a china cow").

s.line: But the strangest of all were the people who lived in this queer country.
s.note: מְשֻׁנֶּה = odd, peculiar. In form it is a pu'al participle of שִׁנָּה (to change), roughly "altered, out of the ordinary". מִכֹּל = "of all": הֲכִי טוֹב מִכֹּל (best of all).

s.line: There were milkmaids and shepherdesses, with brightly colored bodices and golden spots all over their gowns;
s.note: חוֹלֶבֶת (milkmaid) and רוֹעָה (shepherdess) are present participles used as nouns: "one who milks", "one who herds". חוֹלֵב comes from the same root as חָלָב (milk). שֶׁלָּהֶן is the feminine plural "their".

s.line: and princesses with most gorgeous frocks of silver and gold and purple;
s.note: נֶהְדָּר = gorgeous, splendid, a nif'al participle used as an adjective (no passive sense). It is a common word of praise: נֶהְדָּר! = "great!". The noun is הָדָר (splendor).

s.line: and shepherds dressed in knee breeches with pink and yellow and blue stripes down them, and golden buckles on their shoes;
s.note: לָבוּשׁ בְּ… = dressed in …, a pa'ul participle of לָבַשׁ (to wear). לְאָרְכָּם = "along their length", from אֹרֶךְ (length). בִּרְכַּיִם (knees) is another dual.

w: בְּאַבְנֵי חֵן|with gems|~lit. stones of grace
s.line: and princes with jeweled crowns upon their heads, wearing ermine robes and satin doublets;
s.note: מְשֻׁבָּץ (pu'al) = set, inlaid: כֶּתֶר מְשֻׁבָּץ בְּאַבְנֵי חֵן (a crown set with gems). It also means "checkered" (חֻלְצָה מְשֻׁבֶּצֶת), and the pi'el שִׁבֵּץ = to slot someone into a schedule or team. אַבְנֵי חֵן = precious stones.

s.line: and funny clowns in ruffled gowns, with round red spots upon their cheeks and tall, pointed caps.
s.note: מַצְחִיק = funny, literally "making (someone) laugh", the hif'il of צָחַק. מְחֻדָּד = pointed, sharpened; חַד = sharp. מְסֻלְסָל = curly or ruffled: שֵׂעָר מְסֻלְסָל (curly hair).

s.line: And, strangest of all, these people were all made of china, even to their clothes,
and were so small that the tallest of them was no higher than Dorothy’s knee.
s.note: כָּל כָּךְ … שֶׁ… = "so … that …". בֶּרֶךְ (knee) is feminine, like most paired body parts (יָד, רֶגֶל, עַיִן).

s.line: No one did so much as look at the travelers at first, except one little purple china dog with an extra-large head,
s.note: אַף אֶחָד אֲפִלּוּ לֹא … = "no one even …", which is how Hebrew renders "did so much as". בְּמִיּוּחָד = especially, extra: גָּדוֹל בְּמִיּוּחָד = extra-large.

s.line: which came to the wall and barked at them in a tiny voice, afterwards running away again.
s.note: A dog barks עַל someone: נָבַח עֲלֵיהֶם. In slang נָבַח עָלַי means "he snapped at me". זָעִיר = tiny, a little more literary than קְטַנְטַן.

s.line: “How shall we get down?” asked Dorothy.
They found the ladder so heavy they could not pull it up,
s.note: גִּלָּה (pi'el) = to discover, find out; נִתְגַּלָּה / הִתְגַּלָּה = was discovered, turned out. Reported findings keep the present tense: כָּבֵד, מַצְלִיחִים.

s.line: so the Scarecrow fell off the wall and the others jumped down upon him so that the hard floor would not hurt their feet.
s.note: פָּגַע בְּ… = to hurt, hit: תִּפְגַּע לָהֶם בָּרַגְלַיִם "would hurt them in the feet". Hebrew often marks the owner of a body part with לְ: כּוֹאֵב לִי הָרֹאשׁ (my head hurts). פָּגַע also means "to offend": הוּא פָּגַע בִּי.

w: כַּמּוּבָן|of course|~fixed phrase: lit. as understood
s.line: Of course they took pains not to light on his head and get the pins in their feet.
s.note: נִזְהַר = to be careful, a nif'al with active meaning: תִּזָּהֵר! = be careful! לְהִדָּקֵר is the passive nif'al of דָּקַר (to prick, stab): "to be pricked". נָחַת = to land, and a plane's landing is נְחִיתָה.

s.line: When all were safely down they picked up the Scarecrow, whose body was quite flattened out,
s.note: שֶׁהַגּוּף שֶׁלּוֹ = "whose body", literally "that his body". Hebrew has no word for "whose" and uses שֶׁ + a possessive. בְּשָׁלוֹם = safely, in one piece: הִגַּעְנוּ בְּשָׁלוֹם.

s.line: and patted his straw into shape again.
“We must cross this strange place in order to get to the other side,” said Dorothy,
s.note: חָצָה = to cross (a road, a border, a line); חֲצִיָּה = a crossing, and a crosswalk is מַעֲבַר חֲצִיָּה. The same root gives חֵצִי (half).

s.line: “for it would be unwise for us to go any other way except due South.”
s.note: מִצִּדֵּנוּ = "on our part", from צַד (side): זֶה יָפֶה מִצִּדְּךָ (that's nice of you). דָּרוֹמָה = southward: the ending ה shows direction, as in הַבַּיְתָה (homeward).

s.line: They began walking through the country of the china people,
and the first thing they came to was a china milkmaid milking a china cow.
s.note: One root three ways: חָלָב (milk), חָלַב (to milk), חוֹלֶבֶת (a milkmaid). Note פָּרָה → construct פָּרַת: a feminine ה ending becomes ת in the construct.

s.line: As they drew near, the cow suddenly gave a kick and kicked over the stool, the pail, and even the milkmaid herself,
s.note: בָּעֲטָה בְּעִיטָה: verb plus noun from one root, as in קָד קִידָה. בְּעִיטָה is also a kick in football: בְּעִיטָה חָפְשִׁית (a free kick). הָפַךְ = to turn over, overturn; הָפוּךְ = upside down, and also the Israeli name for a latte.

s.line: and all fell on the china ground with a great clatter.
Dorothy was shocked to see that the cow had broken her leg off,
s.note: הִזְדַּעְזֵעַ = to be shocked, shaken (זַעֲזוּעַ = a shock, a jolt). Another hitpa'el swap: after ז the ת turns into ד and moves after it. נִשְׁבַּר (nif'al) = got broken; שָׁבַר (pa'al) = to break something.

s.line: and that the pail was lying in several small pieces, while the poor milkmaid had a nick in her left elbow.
s.note: פְּגָם = a flaw, defect, chip; פָּגוּם = defective, damaged (you will see מוּצָר פָּגוּם, a defective product). שָׁבוּר is the pa'ul participle of שָׁבַר: "broken".

s.line: “There!” cried the milkmaid angrily.
s.note: בְּכַעַס = angrily: בְּ + noun makes an adverb (כַּעַס = anger), like בִּזְהִירוּת (carefully) and בְּשִׂמְחָה.

s.line: “See what you have done!
My cow has broken her leg,

w: כְּדֵי שֶׁיַּדְבִּיקוּ|so that they will glue|hif'il · ד־ב־ק
s.line: and I must take her to the mender’s shop and have it glued on again.
s.note: יַדְבִּיקוּ "they will glue", with no subject, gives Baum's "have it glued": Hebrew uses an impersonal plural where English says "get something done". מְתַקֵּן = a mender, repairman, from תִּקֵּן (to fix); תִּקּוּן = a repair.

w: מָה פִּתְאֹם|what's the idea|~idiom: lit. what suddenly
s.line: What do you mean by coming here and frightening my cow?”
s.note: מָה פִּתְאֹם = "what's the idea?, how dare you?", and on its own it is the everyday "no way!, of course not!": אַתָּה כּוֹעֵס? – מָה פִּתְאֹם!. הִפְחִיד (hif'il) = to frighten, the causative of פָּחַד (to be afraid).

s.line: “I’m very sorry,” returned Dorothy.
“Please forgive us.”
s.note: סָלַח לְ… = to forgive someone, with לְ, not אֶת. סְלִיחָה (sorry, excuse me) is the noun from the same root.

s.line: But the pretty milkmaid was much too vexed to make any answer.
s.note: מִדַּי … מִכְּדֵי + infinitive = "too … to": עָיֵף מִדַּי מִכְּדֵי לָזוּז (too tired to move). In speech people often drop מִכְּדֵי. נִרְגָּז = irritated, annoyed; הִרְגִּיז (hif'il) = to annoy.

w: בְּפַרְצוּף חָמוּץ|sulkily|~idiom: with a sour face
s.line: She picked up the leg sulkily and led her cow away,
s.note: בְּפַרְצוּף חָמוּץ = "with a sour face", sulkily. עָשָׂה פַּרְצוּף = to make a face. חָמוּץ = sour, and מְלָפְפוֹן חָמוּץ is a pickle.

s.line: the poor animal limping on three legs.
s.note: צָלַע = to limp; צוֹלֵעַ = limping. Without vowels צלע is also צֵלָע, a rib or the side of a triangle. שָׁלוֹשׁ (without ה) because רֶגֶל is feminine.

s.line: As she left them the milkmaid cast many reproachful glances over her shoulder at the clumsy strangers,
s.note: הֵעִיף מַבָּט = to cast a glance, literally "make a look fly" (עָף = to fly). תְּעִיף מַבָּט = take a quick look. הִתְרַחֵק (to move away) and הִתְקָרֵב (to come near) are a hitpa'el pair.

s.line: holding her nicked elbow close to her side.
s.note: צָמוּד לְ… = attached, pressed close to; בְּגָדִים צְמוּדִים = tight clothes, and צָמוּד also describes a salary linked to an index, a common news word.

s.line: Dorothy was quite grieved at this mishap.
s.note: תַּקָּלָה = a mishap, glitch, technical fault. You will hear it constantly: תַּקָּלָה טֶכְנִית, הָיְתָה תַּקָּלָה בַּמַּעֲרֶכֶת (there was a fault in the system).

w: טוֹב הַלֵּב|kind-hearted|~lit. good of the heart
s.line: “We must be very careful here,” said the kind-hearted Woodman,
s.note: טוֹב הַלֵּב = kind-hearted: an adjective in construct with a noun, "good of heart". Similar: קְצַר רוּחַ (impatient), רְחַב לֵב (generous). It suits the Woodman, who got his heart from Oz.

s.line: “or we may hurt these pretty little people so they will never get over it.”
s.note: עָלוּל = "liable to, may", used for bad outcomes: עָלוּל לָרֶדֶת גֶּשֶׁם (it may rain). For neutral or good ones Hebrew says עָשׂוּי. הֶחְלִים = to recover (from illness): רְפוּאָה שְׁלֵמָה וְהַחְלָמָה מְהִירָה!.

s.line: A little farther on Dorothy met a most beautifully dressed young Princess,
who stopped short as she saw the strangers and started to run away.
s.note: נֶעֱצַר (nif'al) = to stop, come to a halt. In the news it also means "was arrested": הַחֲשׁוּד נֶעֱצַר (the suspect was arrested). בְּבַת אַחַת = all at once, suddenly.

s.line: Dorothy wanted to see more of the Princess, so she ran after her.
s.note: A trap: רָצְתָה = she wanted (רָצָה, root ר־צ־ה), but רָצָה = she ran (רָץ, root ר־ו־ץ). So רָצָה alone can mean "he wanted" or "she ran"; only context tells them apart.

s.line: But the china girl cried out:
“Don’t chase me!
s.note: רָדַף אַחֲרֵי = to chase, pursue. רְדִיפָה = a chase, and נִרְדָּף = persecuted. אַל + future (תִּרְדְּפִי, feminine) is the negative command.

s.line: Don’t chase me!”
She had such a frightened little voice that Dorothy stopped and said, “Why not?”
s.note: נִשְׁמַע = "sounds", like נִרְאֶה = "looks": זֶה נִשְׁמָע טוֹב (that sounds good). The greeting מָה נִשְׁמָע? ("how's it going?") is literally "what is heard?".

s.line: “Because,” answered the Princess, also stopping, a safe distance away,
“if I run I may fall down and break myself.”
s.note: לְהִשָּׁבֵר is the nif'al infinitive of שׁ־ב־ר: "to get broken". Compare pa'al לִשְׁבֹּר (to break something). After אִם about the future Hebrew uses the future: אִם אָרוּץ = if I (will) run.

s.line: “But could you not be mended?” asked the girl.
s.note: Hebrew often avoids the passive "be mended" with an impersonal phrase: אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְתַקֵּן אוֹתָךְ? "is it impossible to mend you?". אוֹתָךְ is "you" (feminine) as an object.

s.line: “Oh, yes;
but one is never so pretty after being mended, you know,” replied the Princess.
s.note: For "one" in general statements, Hebrew uses a masculine אַתָּה (generic "you") even when a woman is speaking. Right after, אַתְּ יוֹדַעַת is feminine because the Princess is talking to Dorothy. מְתַקְּנִים אוֹתְךָ = "they mend you", impersonal for "being mended".

s.line: “I suppose not,” said Dorothy.
s.note: מַנִּיחַ = to suppose, assume, from הִנִּיחַ (to put down, lay): אֲנִי מַנִּיחַ שֶׁכֵּן (I suppose so). הַנָּחָה = an assumption, and also a discount in a shop.

s.line: “Now there is Mr. Joker, one of our clowns,” continued the china lady,
s.note: בַּדְחָן = a joker, jester, someone who is always kidding around; בְּדִיחָה (a joke) is from the same root. This edition uses it as the clown's name, מַר בַּדְחָן.

s.line: “who is always trying to stand upon his head.
He has broken himself so often that he is mended in a hundred places, and doesn’t look at all pretty.
s.note: The pi'el/pu'al pair: תִּקֵּן = he fixed, תֻּקַּן = it was fixed, מְתֻקָּן = fixed, repaired. מְתֻקָּן also means "proper, decent": חֶבְרָה מְתֻקֶּנֶת (a decent, orderly society).

w: כָּךְ שֶׁתּוּכְלִי|so that you can|pa'al · י־כ־ל
s.line: Here he comes now, so you can see for yourself.”
s.note: בְּעַצְמֵךְ = yourself, on your own (feminine); בְּעַצְמְךָ (masc.), בְּעַצְמִי (myself). תּוּכְלִי is the future of יָכוֹל: "you (f.) will be able".

s.line: Indeed, a jolly little clown came walking toward them,
s.note: אָכֵן = indeed, sure enough, a slightly formal word you'll meet in newspapers. לִקְרָאת = toward, to meet: יָצָא לִקְרָאתָם (went out to meet them), and also "ahead of" a date: לִקְרַאת הַחַג.

s.line: and Dorothy could see that in spite of his pretty clothes of red and yellow and green he was completely covered with cracks,
s.note: לַמְרוֹת = despite, in spite of: לַמְרוֹת הַגֶּשֶׁם, יָצָאנוּ (despite the rain, we went out). מְכֻסֶּה = covered, pu'al of כִּסָּה (to cover).

s.line: running every which way and showing plainly that he had been mended in many places.
s.note: הֶרְאָה = to show, the hif'il (causative) of רָאָה: "made see". בְּבֵרוּר = clearly, certainly; בָּרוּר! = "sure!, obviously".

s.line: The Clown put his hands in his pockets,
s.note: הִכְנִיס = to put in, bring in, the causative of נִכְנַס (to enter). Hebrew usually says "the hands" rather than "his hands" when the owner is obvious.

w: אַחֲרֵי שֶׁנִּפַּח|after he puffed out|pi'el · נ־פ־ח
s.line: and after puffing out his cheeks and nodding his head at them saucily, he said:
s.note: חֻצְפָּה = cheek, nerve, audacity, a word English borrowed (chutzpah); חָצוּף = cheeky, rude. הֵנִיד בָּרֹאשׁ = to nod. נִפַּח = to inflate, puff up; מְנֻפָּח = inflated, and figuratively "pompous".

s.line: “My lady fair,
s.note: Baum's verse is translated with a rhyme in lines 1–2 (יָפָה / צוֹפָה). צָפָה בְּ… = to watch, look on: צוֹפִים בַּטֵּלֶוִיזְיָה; צוֹפֶה = a viewer, and also a Scout.

s.line: Why do you stare
At poor old Mr. Joker?
You’re quite as stiff
And prim as if
You’d eaten up a poker!”
s.note: כְּאִלּוּ = as if; in young people's speech it is also a filler word, like English "like". Baum's poker is a fireplace iron; the Hebrew has a stick, which keeps the picture of a stiff, upright body.

s.line: “Be quiet, sir!” said the Princess.
“Can’t you see these are strangers, and should be treated with respect?”
s.note: הִתְיַחֵס אֶל … = to treat someone, relate to; יַחַס = attitude, treatment (יַחַס טוֹב = good treatment). It also means "to respond to, address": הַשַּׂר לֹא הִתְיַחֵס לַשְּׁאֵלָה (the minister did not address the question).

s.line: “Well, that’s respect, I expect,” declared the Clown,
s.note: Baum rhymes "respect, I expect"; the Hebrew rhymes too: כָּבוֹד / מְאֹד. הִכְרִיז = to declare, announce, a news word: הַמֶּמְשָׁלָה הִכְרִיזָה עַל … (the government announced …); הַכְרָזָה = a declaration.

s.line: and immediately stood upon his head.

w: תָּשִׂימִי לֵב|pay attention|~idiom: lit. put heart
s.line: “Don’t mind Mr. Joker,” said the Princess to Dorothy.
s.note: שָׂם לֵב = to notice, pay attention, literally "put heart": שַׂמְתָּ לֵב? (did you notice?). With אַל it means "don't mind, ignore": אַל תָּשִׂים לֵב.

s.line: “He is considerably cracked in his head, and that makes him foolish.”
s.note: סָדוּק = cracked (סֶדֶק = a crack). The Princess means it literally, but English "cracked" = crazy, too. In Hebrew slang you'd say יֵשׁ לוֹ בֹּרֶג רוֹפֵף, "he has a loose screw". עָשָׂה אוֹתוֹ … = made him …, a colloquial use of עָשָׂה.

s.line: “Oh, I don’t mind him a bit,” said Dorothy.
s.note: מַפְרִיעַ לְ… = to bother, disturb someone, with לְ: אֲנִי לֹא מַפְרִיעַ? (am I interrupting?). הַפְרָעָה = a disturbance.

s.line: “But you are so beautiful,” she continued, “that I am sure I could love you dearly.
s.note: הָיִיתִי יְכוֹלָה = "I could, I would be able": הָיָה + present form makes the conditional ("would"), the same pattern as הָיִיתִי רוֹצָה (I would like).

s.line: Won’t you let me carry you back to Kansas, and stand you on Aunt Em’s mantel?
s.note: הִרְשָׁה = to allow, permit; רְשׁוּת = permission, מֻרְשֶׁה = allowed. הֶעֱמִיד = to stand something up, the causative of עָמַד. A mantel is מַדַּף הָאָח: here אָח is a fireplace (a feminine noun), not אָח "brother".

s.line: I could carry you in my basket.”
s.note: לָשֵׂאת = to carry, the infinitive of נָשָׂא; the נ drops out. The same verb means "to marry" (נָשָׂא אִשָּׁה) and gives נוֹשֵׂא, a topic or subject.

s.line: “That would make me very unhappy,” answered the china Princess.
s.note: אֻמְלָל = miserable, unhappy, a stronger word than לֹא מְאֻשָּׁר. נְסִיכָה → construct נְסִיכַת (princess of), just like פָּרָה → פָּרַת.

w: שֶׁמִּתְחַשֵּׁק לָנוּ|we please|~idiom: lit. that it is desired to us
s.line: “You see, here in our country we live contentedly, and can talk and move around as we please.
s.note: מְרֻצֶּה = satisfied, content, pu'al of רִצָּה (to satisfy): לָקוֹחוֹת מְרֻצִּים (satisfied customers). מִתְחַשֵּׁק לִי = I feel like it: מִתְחַשֵּׁק לִי גְּלִידָה; the slangy version is בָּא לִי. הִסְתּוֹבֵב = to go around, wander about; also to turn around.

s.line: But whenever any of us are taken away our joints at once stiffen, and we can only stand straight and look pretty.
s.note: נִלְקַח is the passive nif'al of לָקַח (to take): "was/is taken". הִתְקַשָּׁה = to harden, stiffen; much more often it means "to have difficulty": הוּא מִתְקַשֶּׁה לְהָבִין (he has trouble understanding). Both come from קָשֶׁה (hard).

w: כַּמּוּבָן|of course|~fixed phrase: lit. as understood
כָּל מָה שֶׁמְּצַפִּים|all that (they) expect|pi'el ptc · צ־פ־ה
s.line: Of course that is all that is expected of us when we are on mantels and cabinets and drawing-room tables,
s.note: צִפָּה מִ… = to expect of someone: מְצַפִּים מִמְּךָ לְהַגִּיעַ בַּזְּמַן (you are expected to come on time). צִפִּיָּה = expectation. Baum's "drawing-room" is today's סָלוֹן, the ordinary Israeli word for a living room.

s.line: but our lives are much pleasanter here in our own country.”
s.note: חַיִּים (life) is always plural in Hebrew, so its adjective is plural too: הַחַיִּים נְעִימִים, חַיִּים טוֹבִים.

w: הָיִיתִי עוֹשָׂה|I would make|pa'al ptc · ע־שׂ־ה
בִּשְׁבִיל כָּל הַכֶּסֶף שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם|for all the world|~idiom: lit. for all the money in the world
s.line: “I would not make you unhappy for all the world!” exclaimed Dorothy.
s.note: לֹא בִּשְׁבִיל כָּל הַכֶּסֶף שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם = "not for all the money in the world", the usual Hebrew way to say "not for anything". שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם = "that is in the world".

s.line: “So I’ll just say good-bye.”
s.note: שָׁלוֹם is both "hello" and "good-bye". פָּשׁוּט = simple, and as an adverb "just, simply": פָּשׁוּט תַּגִּיד לוֹ (just tell him).

s.line: “Good-bye,” replied the Princess.
They walked carefully through the china country.
s.note: בִּזְהִירוּת = carefully, from זָהִיר (careful), like נִזְהַר earlier in the chapter. Signs say זְהִירוּת! = "Caution!".

s.line: The little animals and all the people scampered out of their way, fearing the strangers would break them,
s.note: פִּנָּה (pi'el) = to clear, vacate: פַּנּוּ אֶת הַדֶּרֶךְ! (clear the way!), לְפַנּוֹת אֶת הַדִּירָה (to vacate the apartment). After פָּחֲדוּ שֶׁ comes the future יִשְׁבְּרוּ, as you know.

s.line: and after an hour or so the travelers reached the other side of the country and came to another china wall.
s.note: בְּעֵרֶךְ = approximately, "or so": בְּעֵרֶךְ עֶשֶׂר דַּקּוֹת (about ten minutes). עוֹד before a noun = another, one more: עוֹד כּוֹס קָפֶה.

s.line: It was not so high as the first, however,
and by standing upon the Lion’s back they all managed to scramble to the top.
s.note: הִצְלִיחַ + infinitive = to manage to, succeed in: הִצְלַחְתִּי לִמְצֹא חֲנָיָה (I managed to find parking). הַצְלָחָה! = good luck!

s.line: Then the Lion gathered his legs under him and jumped on the wall;
but just as he jumped, he upset a china church with his tail and smashed it all to pieces.
s.note: הִפִּיל = to drop, knock over, the causative of נָפַל (to fall). נִפֵּץ (pi'el) = to smash, shatter; הִתְנַפֵּץ (hitpa'el) = to shatter by itself. רְסִיסִים = fragments, shards; in the news, רְסִיסִים are shrapnel.

s.line: “That was too bad,” said Dorothy,
s.note: חֲבָל = "too bad, what a pity": חֲבָל שֶׁלֹּא בָּאתָ (too bad you didn't come). חֲבָל עַל הַזְּמַן literally "a pity about the time" is slang for "amazing" or "awful", depending on tone.

w: שֶׁהָיָה לָנוּ|that we had|~lit. there was to us
s.line: “but really I think we were lucky in not doing these little people more harm than breaking a cow’s leg and a church.
s.note: גָּרַם נֵזֶק לְ… = to cause damage to, a phrase you'll see in every news report: הַסְּעָרָה גָּרְמָה נְזָקִים כְּבֵדִים (the storm caused heavy damage). הָיָה לָנוּ מַזָּל = we were lucky.

s.line: They are all so brittle!”
s.note: שָׁבִיר = fragile, breakable: the pattern קָטִיל often means "-able": אָכִיל (edible), קָרִיא (legible), גָּמִישׁ (flexible). Parcels are marked שָׁבִיר!.

s.line: “They are, indeed,” said the Scarecrow,
s.note: בְּהֶחְלֵט = absolutely, definitely, a very common one-word answer: אַתָּה בָּא? – בְּהֶחְלֵט!.

w: אֲסִיר תּוֹדָה|am grateful|~idiom: lit. prisoner of thanks
וְשֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר|and that it is impossible
s.line: “and I am thankful I am made of straw and cannot be easily damaged.
s.note: אֲסִיר תּוֹדָה = grateful, literally "a prisoner of thanks" (אָסִיר = a prisoner); a formal but living phrase: אֲנִי אֲסִיר תּוֹדָה עַל עֶזְרָתְךָ. הִזִּיק לְ… = to harm, damage, from the same root as נֵזֶק (damage).

s.line: There are worse things in the world than being a Scarecrow.”
s.note: מִלִּהְיוֹת = "than being": the comparative מִן attaches to an infinitive too: עָדִיף לָלֶכֶת מִלְּחַכּוֹת (better to walk than to wait). גָּרוּעַ = bad, poor quality; גָּרוּעַ יוֹתֵר = worse.
